cursory

KUR-suh-ree -- three syllables, stress on the first syllable, KUR. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Cursory is hastily done and not thorough.

The customs officer gave the passports only a cursory look before waving the bus through.

Example

The mechanic is already late for lunch, so he gives the engine only a cursory check: pops the hood, glances left, glances right, and slams it shut. 'Looks fine,' he says -- and the worn brake line he never touched fails a week later.

Hastily done and not thorough, the check races across the surface of the task. A cursory glance, read, or inspection almost always carries a warning that something important slipped past.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

hasty: Hasty describes an act or decision made too soon, with too little thought -- a hasty exit, a hasty promise. It blames the rush to act. Cursory is narrower: it describes a look, read, or check that skims a surface too fast to be thorough.

superficial: Superficial says an effort never went below the surface, whatever the reason -- there may have been all the time in the world. Cursory blames the speed: the glance or read was simply over too fast to be thorough.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

thorough: complete and careful in every detail

painstaking: done with extreme, patient care

Where it sits · how little care goes into it

hurried → cursory → perfunctory

hurried vs. cursory: Hurried only says the clock was the problem -- a hurried job might still be decent -- while a cursory one skims the surface so lightly that things get missed.

perfunctory vs. cursory: Perfunctory is the harsher, stronger word: a cursory inspection is too quick, but a perfunctory one adds indifference -- the inspector never cared whether anything was found at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — curs-: to run (Latin currere, cursus)

suffix — -ory: characterized by (Latin -orius)

Put it together: Cursory comes from Latin cursus, 'a running' -- a cursory reading literally runs across the page. The eyes sprint past the words without stopping to check anything, which is exactly why cursory work misses what matters.

Use the root in a new word: cursor: Move the cursor to the end of the line before you start typing.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Cursory clings to nouns of looking and checking: a cursory glance, a cursory read, a cursory inspection. A useful cousin is superficial, a word taught earlier in this course: superficial says the work never went below the surface, while cursory blames the speed -- it was over too fast to be thorough.
